analysis.one_liner: Bans the rule letting skimpy short-term health plans last up to three years.
analysis.headline: The bill to restore the three-month limit on short-term health plans died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite 31 cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2018 rule let insurers sell short-term health plans that last up to 12 months at a time, and up to 36 months with renewals. These plans are exempt from the Affordable Care Act's rules, so they can turn people down or charge more for preexisting conditions and can leave big unpaid bills. The bill would cancel that rule and block agencies from writing a similar one.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance. They would keep access to plans that must cover preexisting conditions and essential benefits, instead of being sold plans that look cheap but can deny care when they get sick.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying their own health insurance

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2018 limit so short-term plans can only cover less than 3 months, including renewals, instead of up to 12 months initially and 36 months total.
Keeps these plans' exemption from Affordable Care Act market rules, such as coverage of preexisting conditions, from becoming a long-term substitute for real coverage.
Bars the Health and Human Services, Treasury, and Labor Departments from implementing the 2018 rule or issuing any substantially similar one.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers that sell short-term plans would lose the ability to market them as lasting up to three years. A smaller number of customers who bought these plans because they cost less than ACA coverage, even though the coverage is thinner, would have to find other options.
analysis.who_pays_short: Short-term insurance sellers and some price-sensitive customers

drawbacks.text: Short-term plans are genuinely cheaper up front, and some people who do not qualify for ACA subsidies or cannot afford fuller coverage buy them; the bill removes that lower-cost option along with its risks.
The bill only nullifies one rule; it does not address the underlying affordability problems in the individual insurance market that push some people toward these plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for consumers is real: plans exempt from preexisting-condition and benefit rules leave people with medical bills exactly when they are sick, and letting them run for three years magnifies that. The cost is that a small group of buyers loses a cheaper, thinner option. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the lost option, but the bill is a narrow fix that does nothing about why those plans attract buyers in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 24, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the action history ends with the committee referral.
It attracted 31 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent, and no Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Short-term health plan insurers kept selling plans of up to 12 months, renewable to 36, under the 2018 rule the bill would have nullified. Consumers who bought those plans kept the risks, and no one got the protections the bill offered.

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Junk Plans Act and led it as sponsor.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; the record shows no action after the committee referral.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but as committee chair never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Short-term, limited-duration health insurers
against.role: Sellers of plans exempt from ACA rules
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the 2018 rule the bill would have nullified, which extended their product from under 3 months to up to 36 months with renewals.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's one Independent-leaning member, and no Republican signed on [S4]; the bill also never received committee action or a floor vote in a Congress where Republicans held 50 Senate seats [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would nullify the 2018 rule that let these plans run up to 12 months, renewable to 36, instead of under 3 months [S2][S3]. These plans profit by selling coverage exempt from ACA rules, including preexisting-condition protections, which leaves enrollees with large bills when they get sick [S2].

Short-term plans draw customers, particularly healthier ones, away from ACA-regulated coverage. Restoring the three-month limit keeps those customers in plans that must cover essential benefits and preexisting conditions [S2].
